sections.title: The Woman's Responsibility and Asking a Torah Scholar
sections.html:
The responsibility for determining the state of impurity and purity rests on the woman: when the veset (menstrual period) begins, she is responsible for telling her husband that she has become impure. And if she saw an appearance about which there is a doubt, the obligation falls on her to ask a Torah scholar, herself or with her husband's help. After she has become impure, the mitzva is upon her to become pure as soon as possible, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:28): "But if she is cleansed of her discharge, then she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be pure"; thus she counts "for herself – by herself" (Ketubot 72a).1

After the Sages agreed to forbid all bloods, distinguishing between blood and another discharge became easier, for what remains is to observe whether the discharge that came out of the womb contains remnants of blood or not. For this purpose the woman must learn to recognize the color of her menstrual blood while it is moist and when it is dry, and from this she will be able to know when the discharge that came out of her womb contains blood and she is forbidden, and when it does not and she is permitted; and in a case of doubt she should ask a Torah scholar. Since young brides are not accustomed to this discernment, as also to other halakhic questions in family purity, the proper guidance for young couples is to ask a Torah scholar about every doubt that arises for them; and after a period of asking questions and becoming accustomed to seeing menstrual blood, the woman will learn to distinguish in most cases between the permitted and the forbidden, and only occasionally, when a doubt arises for her, will she ask a Torah scholar. And there are women who have difficulty deciding, either because their discernment is not sharp, or because by their nature they frequently see borderline appearances, and they must continue to ask in every situation in which they are in doubt. In any event, one must be careful not to be stringent needlessly, and whenever there is a chance that the appearance is pure because of its color or its size, or because its source is a wound, they should ask a Torah scholar; for it is forbidden to be stringent in this, since stringency here causes the neglect of the mitzva of ona (marital relations), which is a great mitzva from the Torah.2

sections.title: The Torah Scholar and How to Ask Him
sections.html:
In order to rule on halakha for the public in matters of appearances of blood, young Torah scholars learn from experienced rabbis, who involve them in viewing the appearances brought before them as questions. After seeing hundreds and thousands of questions from different women with different shades of blood, they learn to distinguish between the forbidden and the permitted.

It is preferable for every couple to establish a Torah scholar whom they will ask regularly, as the Sages said (Avot 1:16): "Make for yourself a teacher and remove yourself from doubt." For when one asks a regular rabbi, one becomes accustomed to analyzing the questions systematically and understanding their solution; but when one goes to different rabbis, one does not learn the method, and many times one is left with doubts. In addition, in cases of problems, out of familiarity and experience the Torah scholar will be able to examine the root of the problem and suggest its solution. Sometimes from the questions he will understand that there is a medical problem, and he will refer the woman for an examination and thereby hasten its solution. If the rabbi to whom the couple is connected is not expert in questions of purity or is too busy, it is better that they establish for themselves an additional rabbi whom they will regularly ask questions in matters of purity.

When a woman is in doubt about an ed bedika (examination cloth), it is good to let it dry and afterward keep it in an envelope, so that the appearance is properly preserved. Since sometimes several questions arise, and one must know the date of each question, one should write next to each ed its date. Examination cloths are not muktze on Shabbat.

When asking a Torah scholar, one should mention all the details related to the question, for example, whether the woman is pregnant, nursing or has a device, and also whether she is taking hormonal pills. If it is an internal bedika, whether it is from the ona close to the veset or from the shiv'a neki'im (the seven clean days), and from which day of the shiv'a neki'im. And if it is a ketem (stain), whether it was accompanied by a sensation or not. One should likewise mention whether there is a wound in the vagina or in the womb, or a concern of a wound, for example if she felt pain during the bedika.

For many generations, in various places, it was accepted that women would bring questions to rabbis, and they did not feel uncomfortable about it. However, in our day, since there are women who feel uncomfortable about it, it is better that when the rabbi receives the questions, the man should bring them to him. And in a place where the rabbanit (rabbi's wife) also assists the rabbi, it is better that the woman bring her questions to the rabbanit, and in a case where the rabbanit is in doubt, she will pass the question on to the rabbi. We have learned from experience that sometimes when a woman asks the rabbanit, in the course of this additional questions in matters of purity and family are resolved for her. However, when there is no possibility for the woman to ask the rabbanit or for the man to ask the rabbi, the woman may ask the rabbi, for in this matter the rabbi serves as a professional who deals in a businesslike manner with the question before him. And just as when necessary one must overcome embarrassment about going to a doctor, so when necessary one must overcome embarrassment about asking a rabbi. And there are rabbis who, in order to make it easier for those asking and to prevent embarrassment, set up a box next to their home in which men and women can place their questions along with a telephone number. And some prefer to ask rabbis and rabbaniyot from various institutes by telephone. However, as I wrote, when there is a possibility, it is preferable to ask a regular rabbi who knows the family, in the spirit of 'make for yourself a teacher,' especially in questions related to family life and its guidance.3

sections.title: The Lighting Suitable for Viewing Appearances
sections.html:
In the past, when the Sages distinguished between impure blood and pure blood, they often needed the best conditions, and then they took care to view the doubtful appearances by sunlight, which makes it possible to see all the shades of color in a balanced way. However, they placed the appearance itself in the shade, for otherwise the strong reflected light of the sun's rays would interfere with seeing the shades of the appearance. Indeed, when necessary, they viewed simple questions also by candlelight, but not by the light of the moon and stars. Even after it was agreed to be stringent and forbid all the shades of blood, ideally they viewed the appearances by day, and only when necessary did they rule by candlelight; and when they had a doubt, they refrained from ruling by candlelight and waited for the morning. When they began to use electric light, the Sages could already answer additional questions at night. Still, in borderline situations one must wait for the day, since fluorescent light is too white, and sometimes impure appearances look pure by its light. On the other hand, the light of an incandescent bulb tends toward yellow-red, and sometimes a pure appearance looks impure by its light. The Torah scholar must be aware of this, and if he is unable to compensate for the bias, he must wait for the morning. With the improvement of electric lighting, it is possible to create light in intermediate shades, similar to daylight, by which almost all doubtful questions can be answered.

One must further pay attention that, whether by day or by night, when one is in a room that has brown and red walls, curtains, furniture and books, doubtful appearances tend to look red and forbidden. However, when the walls, curtains and furniture are white, the color of the appearances is not influenced by them as much.

It is important that every woman, too, be aware of the effect of lighting on the appearance: if she examines at night in a place where the lighting is yellow, or even by day next to a red or brown towel, the appearances look redder. And if the bedika is done by white lighting, the appearances look less red than they really are; and when a slight doubt arises, one should wait for the morning or look at the appearance by balanced lighting.4

sections.title: Changes in the Appearance and Their Law
sections.html:
One may ask about an appearance whether it is moist or dry. And although very rarely it happens that after drying its color changes from a forbidden appearance to a permitted one or the reverse, since these are rare cases, one may rule on the basis of the appearance while it is still moist without waiting for it to dry, for "a judge has only what his eyes see" (Nidda 20b). And such is the custom of all women: according to their bedika in its moist state they decide whether the bedika is pure or impure, and when a doubt arises for them regarding the appearance, they do not hurry to bring it to a Torah scholar while it is still moist.

Sometimes an appearance that was pure while it was moist dries, and the faded color that was in it gathers toward its edges until it looks impure. However, as halakha it should be permitted, because at the time the appearance came out of the womb it was pure, and only as a result of the color particles gathering toward the edges does it look impure at the edges; but if we were to mix it back as it naturally was, it would be pure (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 188:15).5

sections.title: One Who Asks Two Torah Scholars the Same Question
sections.html:
If a Torah scholar ruled that an appearance is impure, another Torah scholar is forbidden to rule that it is pure, for the Sages said (Nidda 20b): "If a Sage declared impure, his colleague may not declare pure; if he forbade, his colleague may not permit." Therefore, one who asked one Torah scholar, and he forbade the appearance to him, should not ask another Torah scholar in order that perhaps he will permit it to him (Avoda Zara 7a). There are two reasons for this: 1) Since halakha has already been decided that the appearance is forbidden, a prohibition has taken effect on it and it cannot be permitted. 2) Because of the honor of the first Torah scholar, for it is not proper to challenge his ruling.

However, when necessary, for example when the one asking is very much seeking a permission for his question, or when the one asking is a Torah scholar who wishes to clarify his question more deeply, the one asking may ask an additional Torah scholar, on condition that he tells him that he has already asked Torah scholar so-and-so, who forbade it. Then, if the second Torah scholar convinces the first Torah scholar that it is proper to permit it, it will be possible to permit it.

What we have learned, that it is forbidden to ask a second Torah scholar, applies specifically to the substance of that same question; but if a new question arises, it is permitted to ask a second Torah scholar who permits, for the prohibition applies only to the substance of the question on which the first one ruled forbidden (Ritva; Radbaz 3:466; Rema YD 242:31).

If the one asking emphasized that he was requesting an opinion and not a halakhic ruling, and the first one expressed his opinion to forbid, he may ask a second Torah scholar, and the second will be permitted to permit it, since no ruling of prohibition on the question issued from the first Torah scholar. And there are Torah scholars who, when they see that in their opinion the question brought before them is forbidden, but it is possible that another Torah scholar would permit it, do not rule that it is forbidden but answer with the words: "I cannot permit it." Then, if the one asking wishes, he may ask a second Torah scholar, who will perhaps permit it.6

sections.title: Guidance and Recommendations for Choosing a Doctor
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for every person to take care of his health, and especially for a woman who is going to give birth, who must make greater efforts, because the life of her fetus also depends on her health. In the past, only in cases of serious complaints by women about pain or heavy bleeding would doctors examine the woman with an internal examination in the vagina. However, in recent generations, with the development of medicine and its division into many fields, a special field of specialization was established for 'women's medicine' (gynecology), and schedules of internal and external examinations were established to prevent illnesses before pregnancy, during pregnancy and after birth, and even after menopause to prevent illnesses such as cancer. In the case of a woman who has difficulty conceiving, there are additional examinations and treatments. Included in the mitzva of guarding one's health, it is a mitzva to undergo the recommended examinations, without exaggerating in concerns and in examinations that are not necessary according to most doctors. In the State of Israel, where today there is good public medicine, one can say that it is a mitzva to undergo the examinations that are funded mainly by the health funds (kupot ḥolim), but there is no need to undergo additional examinations. For if the health funds do not fund them, one can assume that generally they are not essential, and they are intended for cases of special problems, or for people who are more anxious than usual. One who has supplementary insurance has reason to undergo also all the examinations that are funded mainly by the insurance, for since he decided to follow a more stringent line, for him these examinations too are considered regular examinations.

A woman is permitted to be examined by a male doctor, because the doctor is engaged in his work, and his contact with the patient is professional, for the purpose of medicine. In addition, if he were caught behaving immodestly, his livelihood would be harmed. The doctor and the patient must take care not to be alone in a locked room; or it should be known that perhaps one of the staff members will knock on the door to speak with the doctor, and if he does not open, suspicion will arise. When the doctor treats in a place where there are no other people, not even the doctor's wife, the woman should come to the examination with her husband, her sister or her mother.

A God-fearing doctor should be preferred, because the field of women's medicine requires special sensitivity to halakha. For example, when a woman needs contraception during nursing or afterward, the pills intended for this may cause bleeding that renders impure, and the doctor must be aware of this and do everything in his power to prevent this bleeding. Likewise, when fertility treatments or termination of pregnancy are required, one must know the halakha in order to offer the correct treatment. However, when necessary one may go to any doctor, and in a case where a question arises, consult with a rabbi.

In the State of Israel, where public medicine is among the best in the world, for routine treatments it is preferable to go to a doctor who works within the framework of the health fund, both because there is no need to spend money on treatments to which a person is entitled, and because when a person who is not especially wealthy goes for private treatment, there is a concern that in order to save additional payments, he will refrain from necessary examinations and treatments.

It is preferable to go to a regular male or female doctor, because various problems are solved by trial and error, and the better the doctor knows the patient, the better he will know how to fit the correct treatment to her. But if every time a problem arises the patient changes doctors, it is likely that solving the problem will take a long time. However, in special cases there is a need to turn to an additional specialist doctor, and it is preferable to do so in coordination with the regular doctor.

sections.title: Purity after Medical Examinations and Treatments
sections.html:
At first, when the procedures of medical examinations were not clear to the poskim, a concern arose that perhaps doctors sometimes open the womb in their examinations in a way that causes blood to come out. Therefore they instructed every woman who underwent an internal examination to ask the doctor what he had done, and afterward to ask a rabbi whether this examination renders impure. However, in the meantime it has become clear that in every examination or treatment performed without anesthesia, it is clear that the womb was not opened to an extent that might render impure, and the woman is pure without any need to ask a Torah scholar. And even when blood came out as a result of the examination, as long as the examination was not performed during the ona of the veset, she is pure. This is because one should attribute it and assume that it is blood that does not render impure, since it is the blood of a wound that came out of an injury or a cut created during the examination. However, if the blood came out during the ona of her veset, only if she knows with certainty, from her sensation or according to the doctor's testimony, that the blood she saw is due to the examination and not from the veset, is she pure. But if she is in doubt about this, since the blood came out during the ona of her veset, she is impure.

Even when the treatment takes place inside the womb, such as during the insertion or removal of an 'intrauterine device,' or when the treatment is intended for cutting and removing growths, the woman does not become impure, for the blood that comes out as a result of this procedure is the blood of a wound and a cut and not menstrual blood. However, if the treatment was performed during the ona of her veset, there is a concern that menstrual blood is also mixed in the blood she saw, and therefore, as long as the woman does not have certainty that the blood she saw does not also contain menstrual blood, she is impure (above, 2:13–14).

The only medical treatment that certainly renders impure is a curettage in connection with a miscarriage, in which the uterine lining that was meant to sustain the fetus is removed, and the law of the bleeding that comes out in it is like the law of menstrual bleeding, in which the uterine lining also breaks down and comes out.7
